rules.title: Fair Chance in Housing Act (criminal-record screening limits)
rules.requirement: Housing providers may not put criminal-record questions on a housing application, or ask about criminal records orally or in writing, before making a conditional offer. Two exceptions apply: methamphetamine manufacture on federally assisted premises, and lifetime sex-offender registration. Before or after an offer, providers may never evaluate arrests or charges without conviction, expunged, pardoned, vacated or nullified convictions, juvenile adjudications, or sealed records. After a conditional offer they may consider only: (1) convictions for listed serious crimes or lifetime-registration offenses; (2) first-degree indictable offenses within 6 years; (3) second- or third-degree offenses within 4 years; and (4) fourth-degree offenses within 1 year. Each lookback runs from the conviction or the end of the prison sentence. A conditional offer may be withdrawn only on a preponderance-of-evidence finding that withdrawal is necessary to a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest. That finding requires an individualized assessment of the listed factors. A withdrawal requires written notice with specific reasons and an opportunity to appeal by offering evidence. The applicant may request the information relied on within 30 days, and the provider must supply it free within 10 days. Before accepting any application fee, the provider must disclose in writing whether criminal history is reviewed and that the applicant may submit evidence of inaccuracy or rehabilitation. Discriminatory advertising about criminal records is barred, as is any other dissemination or use of the records. Providers may not require drug or alcohol tests or ask for consent to obtain drug-treatment records. Enforcement is only through complaints to the Division on Civil Rights, not court actions, with a 14-day mediation opportunity. Penalties are up to $1,000, $5,000 or $10,000 depending on prior violations. The Director may order return of the application fee and payment of up to $1,000 to the applicant.
rules.key_value: No criminal-history inquiry before conditional offer; post-offer lookback 6 yrs (1st degree) / 4 yrs (2nd-3rd degree) / 1 yr (4th degree), no limit for listed serious crimes and lifetime registration; records request within 30 days, provider responds free within 10 days; penalties up to $1,000 / $5,000 / $10,000

rules.title: Residential rental application fee cap ($50, CPI-adjusted)
rules.requirement: A landlord or its agent may not require an application or similar fee above $50 to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes. Starting January 1 of the year after enactment (January 1, 2027), the cap is adjusted each year in proportion to the CPI-U for New York-Northern New Jersey-Long Island, All Items. The adjustment is made only if the percent change is greater than zero. The State Treasurer determines it by December 1, and the Director of Consumer Affairs publishes the limit. Penalties are up to $500 for a first offense, $750 for a second and $1,000 for each later offense. They are enforced by summary proceedings in the Superior Court, Special Civil Part, on complaint of the Director of Consumer Affairs or the Attorney General. The amount wrongfully charged is remitted to the applicant. The Director must adopt rules, including a mechanism for reporting violations.
rules.key_value: Max application fee $50 (CPI adjustment beginning January 1, 2027); penalties up to $500 / $750 / $1,000 per offense; overcharge remitted to applicant

rules.title: New Jersey Security Deposit Law
rules.requirement: A landlord may collect a security deposit of no more than 1.5 times one month's rent. Any pet deposit and any prepaid rent held as security, including last month's rent, count toward this cap. At lease inception the landlord may require at most the 1.5-month deposit plus the first month's rent, 2.5 months in total. Any yearly increase in the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. The deposit remains the tenant's property and must be held in trust, not commingled. It must be kept in an interest-bearing account at an insured New Jersey institution. Landlords holding deposits for 10 or more units may instead use an insured New Jersey-based money market fund. Interest belongs to the tenant and is paid or credited annually. The landlord must give written notice of the institution, amount, account type and interest rate within 30 days of receipt, at each annual interest payment, and on any transfer. If notice or interest is not provided, the tenant may have the deposit plus 7% annual interest applied to rent after written notice. The deposit plus interest, less itemized deductions for damage beyond normal wear and tear and other sums due, must be returned within 30 days after the tenancy ends. Deductions must be itemized and returned by personal delivery or registered or certified mail. Return is due within 5 business days when the tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation. It is due within 15 business days after a Safe Housing Act termination. A new owner is responsible for the deposit. Wrongful withholding exposes the landlord to double the amount withheld plus costs and attorney's fees. There are civil penalties of $500 to $2,000 for willfully withholding deposits of tenants receiving public assistance, and disorderly-persons liability for unlawful use of deposit money.
rules.key_value: Max 1.5x monthly rent (2.5x including first month's rent at lease start); annual increase max 10% of current deposit; return within 30 days (5 business days if displaced; 15 business days after Safe Housing Act termination); double damages plus fees; 7% per annum applied to rent if notice or interest not provided

rules.title: New Jersey Anti-Eviction Act (good cause eviction)
rules.requirement: A residential landlord may not evict a tenant, or fail to renew a written or oral lease, without good cause, and must prove the cause in court. The statutory causes are: nonpayment; disorderly conduct; willful or grossly negligent damage; substantial breach of rules or lease covenants; nonpayment of a rent increase that is not unconscionable and complies with municipal rent control; health and safety violations, illegal occupancy or government redevelopment; permanent retirement from residential use; refusal of reasonable lease changes; habitual late payment; condominium, cooperative or fee-simple conversion; owner or buyer occupancy after conversion or in small buildings; end of employment-based tenancy; and certain drug, assault, terroristic-threat, theft and human-trafficking offenses. A written Notice to Quit is required for every cause except nonpayment, and a Notice to Cease must first be given for some causes. Only a court judgment and warrant for removal executed by a court officer can remove a tenant; self-help evictions and lockouts are illegal. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy are owed relocation assistance of six times the monthly rent. The landlord must pay it at least five days before removal, or the municipality pays from a revolving fund and the landlord repays it. A landlord who evicts for personal occupancy but does not occupy the unit for 6 months faces treble damages plus fees. A landlord who evicts to board up, demolish or retire a property and then returns it to residential use within 5 years faces treble damages plus fees and a civil penalty of up to $10,000. Owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings may be evicted only for a narrower list of causes. Rooming and boarding house owners must follow the same good cause and notice rules and give the County Welfare Board at least 3 working days' notice. A landlord who has not registered as required cannot obtain an eviction.
rules.key_value: Notice to Quit: none for nonpayment (14 days in federally subsidized housing); 3 days (disorderly conduct, damage, employment end, drug/assault/theft offenses); 1 month (rule or lease breach, rent increase, lease changes, habitual late payment); 2 months (post-conversion or small-building owner/buyer occupancy); 3 months (health/safety removal); 18 months (retirement from residential use); 3 years (conversion). Relocation assistance for illegal occupancy: 6x monthly rent. Treble damages; civil penalty up to $10,000.

rules.title: Foreclosure tenant protections and notices (Foreclosure Fairness Act)
rules.requirement: Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction; residential tenants stay with the property when a lender or buyer takes possession. A buyer of a foreclosed property who wants to occupy it as a primary residence must give a 90-day notice to quit. A tenant whose lease runs longer may not be evicted until the lease expires. Month-to-month tenants and tenants in owner-occupied two- and three-family units are covered by the 90-day notice. Anyone acquiring a foreclosed property with rental units must notify tenants in English and Spanish within 10 business days after the sale that ownership has changed and they need not move. In buildings with 10 or fewer units the notice is addressed to each tenant, posted on each door and mailed by certified and regular mail. In buildings with more than 10 units it is posted in a prominent location. Foreclosing creditors must give the court-rule 'Notice to Residential Tenants of Rights During Foreclosure'. Any monetary offer to induce a tenant to leave must come with a separate notice and a five-day review period, and acceptance must be in writing. Pressure tactics are barred. These include misrepresenting rights, harassment, cutting utilities, failing to maintain the property, and rent increases above rent control or unconscionable increases.
rules.key_value: 90-day notice to quit; tenant notice within 10 business days after sale (English and Spanish); 5-day review period for buyout offers

rules.title: Reprisal (anti-retaliation) protections for tenants
rules.requirement: A landlord may not retaliate against a tenant by eviction, substantial alteration of the lease or its terms, or refusal to renew a lease when the tenant exercises protected rights. Protected rights are: enforcing rights under the lease or State or local law; making a good-faith complaint to a governmental authority about a health or safety violation after first notifying the landlord in writing and allowing a reasonable time to correct it; organizing or joining a lawful organization, including a tenant organization; and refusing lease changes made in retaliation for these actions. The tenant may sue for damages.

rules.title: Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act (condominium/cooperative conversion protections, including the bar on conversion-cost rent increases)
rules.requirement: Eligible tenants in a building being converted to condominium, cooperative or fee-simple ownership may obtain a protected tenancy that shields them from eviction for up to 40 years. Eligible tenants are those aged 62 or older before the conversion recording date, permanently disabled tenants, and qualifying service-disabled veterans. They must have lived in the building at least one year before the conversion recording date. Household income must not exceed three times the county average per-person income or $50,000, whichever is greater. The landlord or converter must notify tenants of their right to apply. Applications are generally due within 60 days to the designated municipal official or administrative agent. Protected tenants are shielded from changes in tenancy terms or rent increases resting solely on the conversion. For all tenants in a converted building, protected or not, rents may not be increased to cover costs resulting solely from the conversion. Increases for new services or amenities remain allowed. The Tenant Protection Act of 1992 extends similar protected tenancy to qualified tenants in qualified counties; Hudson County is currently the only one.

rules.title: Law Against Discrimination: source of lawful income and other protected characteristics in rental
rules.requirement: The New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (LAD) bars housing discrimination in sale or rental based on source of lawful income or source of lawful rent or mortgage payment. It also bars discrimination based on race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, marital, civil union or domestic partnership status, familial status, affectional or sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, disability and nationality. A landlord may not deny a Section 8 voucher holder the right to rent based solely on that source of income. Discriminatory advertising is barred. A landlord may still refuse to rent for insufficient income, a family too large for the unit, occupancy that would violate zoning, or poor credit history. Complaints may be filed free with the Division on Civil Rights within 180 days, or in Superior Court within two years. Penalties run up to $10,000 for a first offense.

rules.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
rules.requirement: Five acts are made unlawful and violations of the New Jersey Antitrust Act: (a) for a rental property owner or its agent, representative or subcontractor to subscribe to, contract for, or exchange any consideration for the services of a coordinator; (b) for a coordinator to facilitate an agreement among rental property owners that restricts competition, including by performing a coordinating function; (c) for two or more persons to engage in or facilitate parallel pricing coordination; (d) for an agent or representative of a coordinator to engage in parallel pricing coordination; (e) for any person to perform a coordinating function. A coordinating function means using algorithms or automated processes on the nonpublic, competitively sensitive information of two or more owners, or of any other owner, to set or recommend rents, material lease terms or occupancy levels. It also covers recommending such terms to two or more owners from the same or a substantially similar algorithm in a way that facilitates parallel pricing coordination. Antitrust Act remedies (C.56:9-6 to 9-17) apply. The Attorney General must establish a complaint location and may adopt rules. Municipalities may not enact ordinances that conflict with the act.
rules.key_value: Effective 2027-07-01; violations are New Jersey Antitrust Act violations (C.56:9-6 to 9-17 remedies); AG complaint portal; conflicting municipal ordinances prohibited

coverage.landlord_size_condition: Applies to any rental property owner owning, directly or indirectly, one or more rental residential dwelling units; controlling-interest holders are treated as a single owner with the entity.
coverage.summary: Covers residential dwelling units in New Jersey: any house, apartment, accessory unit or other unit intended as a primary residence. Inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities are excluded. Applies to owners, their agents and coordinators (software and data providers).
coverage.other_conditions: The following are not a coordinating function: research, statistical or testing use not used to set terms; free public rent estimates; equal-terms brokerage listing databases that do not set or recommend terms or collect sensitive data to do so; and government affordability controls. Not an algorithmic device: spreadsheets operating without AI that require human analysis, and databases that only query unprocessed data.

rules.exemptions: Research, statistical or testing uses; free public rent estimates; equal-terms real estate brokerage databases; government affordability controls (governments are not coordinators); non-AI spreadsheets requiring human analysis; databases that only query unprocessed data.
